summary:
We started with a question: how can we keep track of an astronaut’s health without asking them to stop what they’re doing to take measurements all day? Our idea was to collect as much as possible during sleep, use wearables for some readings, and leave exams for scheduled check-ups or when the medical team needs them.

We built Ares Health to try out that idea. You can pick a Mars, Moon, or Earth orbit mission, or create your own by choosing the stages, dates, durations, and communication delays. In the Mars mission, you can try 16 scenarios. Change a reading on a specific day and see what happens to the graph, who gets an alert, and when it reaches Earth. The commander, medical team, engineers, and Earth mission control each see the information they need to respond.
details:
When we planned Ares Health, we wanted most of the collection to happen while the astronaut was asleep. We imagined a sleep station that could track things like breathing and movement overnight. Wearables could fill in some of the gaps. Exams such as blood tests and bone density scans would happen separately, at scheduled check-ups or when needed. We also wanted the astronaut to be able to say what they were feeling. If your knee hurts after training, you should be able to record where it hurts and indicate how urgent it is.

An important part of our idea was to give each astronaut a starting point from their check-up on Earth. That way, the crew can look at what changed for that person over time. The commander can see what needs attention today. The medical team can open the history, check when a reading was taken, and record changes to restrictions, allergies, or the care plan. Engineers can investigate an incomplete reading or a sensor fault. If an urgent symptom is reported during a communications outage, the onboard team can see the alert while the message to Earth is still waiting. We used the same communications model for messages from family.

We built the first version around a 990-day Mars mission and gave it 16 scenarios to test. Then we added Moon and Earth orbit missions and an editor so people can make their own. You choose the stages, when each one happens, how long it lasts, and how long a message takes to reach Earth. Each mission keeps its own edits in the browser. To see how the simulation works, open the high cabin CO₂ case and change the reading from 3.20 to 2.50 mmHg. The graph updates and the engineering alert clears.

NASA’s Human Research Program helped us decide which problems to model. We used NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 for the one-hour cabin CO₂ example and NASA’s Human Performance reference for selected comparisons with preflight measurements. NASA’s OSD-280 study gave us context for including salivary microbiome diversity as a research indicator.

We built the website with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses fictional readings for 41 indicators. The proposed sensors and exams are simulated, and medication entries represent decisions made by a simulated clinician. We used OpenAI Codex to help with research, coding, scenario development, testing, design, and editing this submission. We also used OpenAI image generation for the labeled Earth image in the family-message scenario.
